extracted.intended_audience: in-house PR/marketing professionals, startup and company communicators writing press releases (from small startups to Fortune 500s)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, formatting, and distributing company press releases to earn media pickup and serve as owned marketing content. Covers elements to include, voice/style, examples by announcement type, and distribution best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and audience of a press release
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release is an official written statement that an organization sends to the news media; primary audience is news outlets, though releases live on the internet and are visible to stakeholders and customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include enough information so news outlets can publish their own story or request an interview. Think of releases both as a ticket to earned media and as valuable digital marketing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / length
rubrics_metrics.description: Most press releases are succinct, just one to two pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the release focused — reporters don’t have time for long intros or fluffy background. Use the reverse pyramid (most important first) to prioritize information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential structural elements (format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard press release format: contact information and ‘For Immediate Release’ at the top; title and italicized subheading; a dateline; an opening line sharing the key details; two to three paragraphs to add context and additional details; bulleted facts/figures; a company boilerplate at the bottom; three pound symbols (###) to signify the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format in a newsy, straightforward way so a journalist can imagine it as an article. Use bullets for scannability. The tradition of ### at the end is still adopted and highly respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific required items to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Every press release should include: your contact information (top or bottom), the phrase 'For immediate release' (top right), a dateline (city and state in all caps followed by the release date), a headline that explains the announcement, your business location in the first sentence, a boilerplate at the end, and a clear end marker (e.g., ###).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these so journalists can quickly find key details and follow up; dateline format per AP Style; boilerplate should include a website link.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP Style adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Format and write your press release in AP (Associated Press) Style, which most newspapers and online media sites use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP Style governs grammar, city and state abbreviations, address formatting, title formatting, and when to spell out or use figures for numbers. Using AP Style makes it easier for outlets to pick up your piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A great headline should grab attention and summarize the key news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use action verbs; avoid vague words like 'exciting'; be specific; keep it short; make it interesting. Look for data or connections to current events. Be playful only if it fits the brand and topic. Invest time — reporters receive many releases daily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheadline purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The subheadline adds context and gives readers a better idea of the news you're sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand slightly but keep it tight; it can be a short paragraph or bullet points and must support the headline to entice readers to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede / first paragraph content
rubrics_metrics.description: The first paragraph should state what the announcement is about while providing context and answering who, what, when, where, and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the most critical information. Use the reverse pyramid: most important info first, then supporting details. Journalists need facts they can use to tell the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up paragraphs (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The next two to three paragraphs should expand context and include quotes explaining the 'why' behind the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide background that supports the lede but avoid fluff. Use quotes and supporting facts to add credibility and perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A boilerplate is a short description of your company and what it offers placed at the end of the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it under 100 words; use clear, plain language; link to your website; summarize 'who' and 'what' succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business location in lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your business location in the first sentence of the press release (the dateline accomplishes this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps journalists and local outlets quickly determine geographic relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of voice: formal vs informal
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional press releases are written in third person; however, first-person (I/We) and active voice can be appropriate depending on brand voice and industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal third-person is still appropriate for investor disclosures and formal industries; consider active voice and first-person to personalize the brand. Match tone to your audience and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Include at least one quote from a spokesperson, client, or executive to provide context and explain why the news matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose speakers intentionally (CEO, founder, project lead). Avoid bland executive quotes, jargon, and hyperbole. Customer quotes are often more powerful than generic executive statements; use action words and concrete examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Include high-quality multimedia assets (images, video, infographics) with the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV stations need strong visuals; providing multimedia makes journalists more likely to pick up a release. Offer several high-quality images and, when possible, video or data visualizations to increase chances of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulleted facts and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bulleted facts/figures to make key points quickly scannable for journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bullets help share statistics, takeaways, or quick facts; useful in subheads or within the body to highlight important data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and clarity testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread the release and test clarity with a colleague who reads it cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix typos and formatting issues; if a colleague cannot explain the news clearly after one read, rewrite. Consider using editing tools (including AI tools) to ideate and polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Templates: structure with flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use press release templates to ensure you include essential elements while allowing flexibility to sound unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates save time and reduce guesswork but customize to add new data, graphics, or creative angles so you don't sound like everyone else.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'So, what?' — newsworthiness and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: A release must answer why readers should care — explain the impact and make the relevance explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out relevance for the outlet's audience; localize national stories for regional outlets and provide local data or angles. This answers 'So, what?' and 'Why now?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsjacking and 'Why now?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect your press release to trending news or current events to increase value to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use newsjacking carefully to show timeliness and relevance; explicitly state the connection so journalists see the angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Common distribution methods include wire services, email distribution to targeted journalists, and owned media distribution (posting on company website and social channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire services provide broad reach and allow geographic/industry targeting; email lets you pitch specific journalists; owned media boosts SEO and reaches existing audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted journalist outreach / personalized pitches
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than blasting every journalist, reach out to a few who are a good fit and send personalized messages that explain why the story matters to their audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect the dots for the reporter; show relevance to their beat or geography. Personalization increases pickup likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes and exclusives
rubrics_metrics.description: You can send embargoed releases to give journalists time to craft stories or offer an exclusive to one outlet for first access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state embargo terms (when content can be published). Use exclusives or embargoes strategically for special circumstances to create relationships or deeper coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing strategy for release
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid publishing on the top of the hour because many companies schedule releases then; choose distinct times and consider time zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staggered release times (e.g., 1:12 p.m. or 3:18 p.m.). Earlier in the day is usually better, particularly if targeting EST/European markets from the West Coast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-pickup amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: When your release gets media coverage, amplify it by sharing coverage on email and social to create a second wave of distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party stories are more credible; sharing them also helps journalists (social metrics can factor into their reviews), which can earn you future favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product launch press release content
rubrics_metrics.description: Product launch releases should emphasize the product's specs, pricing, availability, and other consumer-relevant details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain what the product does, features, pricing, availability date, where it can be purchased; share the problem you solve and use credible research to position it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mergers and acquisitions content
rubrics_metrics.description: M&A announcements should include details about all organizations involved, information about the transaction, and quotes from leadership teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough detail to inform stakeholders about growth/trajectory; be factual and include leadership reaction/next steps as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product update press release content
rubrics_metrics.description: Product updates should explain what changed, why the change was made, and how it benefits users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on user impact and concrete benefits rather than internal process details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotions press release content and frequency caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion releases (e.g., discounts, giveaways) can be used to spread the word but should be selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on a few big promotions each quarter; journalists may stop opening your emails if you send releases for every minor discount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event press release content
rubrics_metrics.description: Event releases should state what the event is about, who should attend, when and where it will be held, and pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly communicate significance and any ticketing or registration details journalists or readers need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand opening press release content
rubrics_metrics.description: For new office openings, relocations, or first openings, announce date, location, who is involved, freebies/activities, and reason for the move if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include details that make the opening newsworthy and any public-facing elements (freebies, ceremonies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnership press release content and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Partnership announcements should summarize each partner, explain why the partnership was created, who benefits, and other key details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work closely with partners for approval on content and include quotes and boilerplates from both companies when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebranding press release content
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebrand releases should explain what the change is, why it's happening, and why it matters; tie in executive quotes and reintroduce company values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the release to reduce confusion and reframe the brand narrative; be explicit about implications for customers or stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership change press release content and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive change releases should be concise and neutral; if possible, provide a high-level reason for the change, interim leadership details, and a bio/photo of the incoming leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public companies, announce quickly and adhere to regulatory requirements; keep tone neutral in sensitive situations to avoid deepening a crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and milestones press release content
rubrics_metrics.description: Award or milestone releases should state the company achievement, explain why the award/milestone matters, and include ceremony details if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate why the recognition is meaningful and link to supporting data or context to avoid sounding merely self-congratulatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro tips for headline/subhead drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: When stuck on a headline or subhead, either add a placeholder and return later or use the 'So, what?' exercise to clarify the key message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple exercise clarifying why the story matters can help craft a stronger headline and subhead on revision.
